# Summary of the 1997 Conservative Party Manifesto

The 1997 Conservative Party Manifesto, introduced by Prime Minister John Major, presented a vision for Britain's continued economic prosperity and social stability following 18 years of Conservative governance.

## Economic Achievements and Vision

The manifesto highlighted Britain's transformation from the "sick man of Europe" to its most successful economy. Key accomplishments included record low unemployment (lower than any major European economy), inflation below 4% for over four years, and mortgage rates at 30-year lows. The Conservatives aimed to maintain public spending below 40% of national income while targeting a 20p basic rate of income tax.

## Opposition to European Integration

A central theme was resistance to deeper European integration. The Conservatives opposed the Social Chapter, which they argued would impose continental-style regulations destroying British jobs. They guaranteed a referendum before any decision to join a single European currency and pledged to protect Britain's border controls, veto powers, and budget rebate.

## Family and Welfare Policies

The manifesto proposed significant tax reforms to support families, including allowing non-working spouses to transfer unused personal tax allowances to working partners caring for children or elderly relatives. Revolutionary pension reforms would provide young workers with personal pension funds through national insurance rebates, aiming to reduce dependence on state pensions.

## Public Services

The Conservatives pledged year-on-year increases in NHS funding, expansion of medical school intakes, and support for GP fundholding. In education, they promised a "guarantee" of standards with intervention in failing schools, alongside expanded school choice including grammar schools and specialist schools.

## Law and Order

Tough-on-crime policies included mandatory minimum sentences for persistent burglars and drug dealers, 10,000 new CCTV cameras, and measures to tackle juvenile crime through Parental Control Orders and faster youth court procedures.

## Constitutional Stability

The party strongly opposed devolution for Scotland and Wales, arguing it would threaten the Union. They favoured evolutionary constitutional change over Labour's "revolutionary" proposals, rejecting proportional representation and a Bill of Rights.

The manifesto concluded with 25 pledges encapsulating their vision of low taxes, strong families, quality public services, and national sovereignty.
